question: How do you pass a parameter to an event handler?
answerGeneral: Wrap the handler in an arrow function so the parameter is applied when the event fires: onClick={() => handleClick(id)}. Writing onClick={handleClick(id)} is the common mistake — that calls the function during render instead of on click. The arrow function also gives you the event itself if you need it: onClick={e => handleClick(id, e)}. Each render creates a new arrow function, which is usually fine and only worth optimising if profiling shows it matters.
detailMd:
## The arrow-function wrapper To call a handler with an argument, wrap it so the call happens when the event fires, not during render: ```jsx {items.map((item) => (
  • handleClick(item.id)}> {item.label}
    • ))} ``` ## The classic mistake ```jsx
  • // wrong ``` This calls `handleClick` during render and passes its return value as the handler. The click does nothing — and if the function sets state, you get an infinite render loop. `onClick` needs a function, not a function's result. ## Getting the event too The wrapper still has access to the event: ```jsx handleChange(id, e.target.value)} /> ``` ## In class components The other form is `.bind`: `onClick={this.handleClick.bind(this, item.id)}` — same effect, partially applying the argument. ## The performance footnote A new arrow function is created every render. This is almost always irrelevant. It only matters when the handler is passed to a `React.memo` child, where a fresh function defeats the memo — there you wrap it in `useCallback`. Do not pre-optimise this; fix it only when profiling points at it.
answerGeneralTr: Handler'ı bir arrow function'a sar, böylece parametre event tetiklendiğinde uygulanır: onClick={() => handleClick(id)}. onClick={handleClick(id)} yazmak yaygın hatadır — bu fonksiyonu tıklamada değil render sırasında çağırır. Arrow function ayrıca ihtiyacın olursa event'in kendisini de verir: onClick={e => handleClick(id, e)}. Her render yeni bir arrow function oluşturur; bu genelde sorun değildir ve yalnızca profiling önemli olduğunu gösterirse optimize etmeye değer.

question: What is the purpose of the callback argument of setState?
answerGeneral: In class components setState is asynchronous — the new state is not visible on the very next line. The optional second argument is a callback that React runs after the state update has been applied and the component has re-rendered, so it is the safe place to read the updated value or trigger a follow-up. In function components there is no setState callback; you use a useEffect that depends on the state value instead.
detailMd:
## setState is asynchronous

In a class component, `setState` does not update `this.state` on the spot. React batches updates and applies them before the next render, so reading state right after setting it gives the old value:

```jsx
this.setState({ count: this.state.count + 1 });
console.log(this.state.count); // still the old value
```

## The callback argument

`setState` takes an optional second argument — a function React runs after the update is applied and the component has re-rendered:

```jsx
this.setState({ query: term }, () => {
  console.log(this.state.query); // updated value, guaranteed
  this.fetchResults();
});
```

It is the reliable place to read the new state or trigger follow-up work that depends on it.

## Updater function vs callback

Do not confuse the two arguments. The first can be an updater function — `setState((prev) => ...)` — for computing the next state from the previous. The second is the after-render callback. They solve different problems.

## In function components

There is no `setState` callback. The equivalent is a `useEffect` that lists the state value as a dependency — it runs after the render that applied the change:

```jsx
useEffect(() => { fetchResults(); }, [query]);
```
answerGeneralTr: Class component'lerde setState asenkrondur — yeni state hemen sonraki satırda görünmez. Opsiyonel ikinci argüman, React'in state güncellemesi uygulandıktan ve component yeniden render olduktan sonra çalıştırdığı bir callback'tir; yani güncellenmiş değeri okumak ya da bir takip işlemi tetiklemek için güvenli yerdir. Function component'lerde setState callback'i yoktur; bunun yerine o state değerine bağlı bir useEffect kullanırsın.

question: What happens when you call setState?
answerGeneral: setState, or a useState setter, does not mutate state immediately. React merges or replaces the value, marks the component and its descendants as needing to re-render, and schedules the work. It then re-renders, builds a fresh virtual tree, diffs it against the previous one, and commits only the minimal real DOM changes. Multiple updates in the same event are batched into one render for efficiency, which is why a state read right after a set still shows the old value.
detailMd:
## It schedules, it does not mutate

Calling `setState` (class) or a `useState` setter (function) does not change state immediately. React records the requested change, marks the component as needing to re-render, and schedules the work.

## The render-and-commit cycle

On the next tick React recomputes the new state, re-renders the component to produce a new element tree, diffs that tree against the previous one (reconciliation), and commits only the minimal set of real DOM changes. Children re-render too, unless they are memoised and their props are unchanged.

## Batching

Multiple updates in the same event handler are batched into a single render:

```jsx
setCount(count + 1);
setFlag(true);
// one re-render, not two
```

Since React 18 this batching also covers updates inside promises and timeouts.

## Why a read after a set is stale

Because the update is scheduled, the state variable in the current scope is unchanged for the rest of that render — it is a snapshot. To build on the latest value, use the updater form: `setCount((c) => c + 1)`. This is also why mutating state directly does nothing visible: React compares by reference and never sees the change.
answerGeneralTr: setState ya da bir useState setter'ı state'i anında değiştirmez. React değeri merge eder ya da değiştirir, component'i ve alt elemanlarını yeniden render gerektiriyor olarak işaretler ve işi planlar. Sonra yeniden render eder, taze bir virtual ağaç kurar, onu öncekiyle karşılaştırır ve yalnızca minimum gerçek DOM değişikliğini uygular. Aynı event içindeki birden fazla güncelleme verimlilik için tek bir render'da batch'lenir; bu yüzden bir set'ten hemen sonraki state okuması hâlâ eski değeri gösterir.

question: How are events handled in React?
answerGeneral: You attach handlers with JSX props like onClick or onChange, passing a function. React does not bind a listener to each DOM node — it uses one delegated listener at the root and dispatches events through its own system. The event object you receive is a SyntheticEvent, a cross-browser wrapper over the native event with the same API, so behaviour is consistent everywhere. Handler names are camelCase, and you pass the function itself, not a string.
detailMd:
## Attaching handlers

You attach an event handler with a JSX prop — camelCased — and pass it a function:

```jsx
<button onClick={handleClick}>Save</button>
<input onChange={(e) => setValue(e.target.value)} />
```

You pass the function itself, not a string and not a call.

## SyntheticEvent

The argument your handler receives is a `SyntheticEvent` — React's cross-browser wrapper around the native DOM event. It exposes the same API (`preventDefault`, `stopPropagation`, `target`) but behaves identically across browsers, so you do not write per-browser workarounds. `e.nativeEvent` reaches the underlying event if needed.

## Delegation under the hood

React does not attach a listener to every DOM node. It attaches one listener at the app root and dispatches events through its own system. This is efficient and means handlers keep working as the tree changes — you never manage `addEventListener` and `removeEventListener` yourself.

## Things to know

- Returning `false` from a handler does nothing — call `e.preventDefault()` explicitly.
- Handlers run on the React tree, so a portalled child's events bubble to its React parent.
- For listeners on `window` or `document`, use a `useEffect` and remove the listener in its cleanup.
answerGeneralTr: Handler'ları onClick ya da onChange gibi JSX prop'larıyla, bir fonksiyon geçerek bağlarsın. React her DOM node'una bir listener bağlamaz — kökte tek bir delege edilmiş listener kullanır ve event'leri kendi sistemi üzerinden dağıtır. Aldığın event object'i bir SyntheticEvent'tir; native event üzerinde, aynı API'ye sahip, cross-browser bir sarmalayıcıdır, böylece davranış her yerde tutarlıdır. Handler adları camelCase'tir ve string değil fonksiyonun kendisini geçersin.

question: Where should you make an AJAX request in a component?
answerGeneral: In a function component, data fetching belongs in a useEffect, typically with an empty dependency array so it runs once after mount — the equivalent of the old componentDidMount. You set the result into state, and you handle cleanup (aborting the request) in the effect's return so a fast unmount does not set state on a gone component. In practice most apps delegate this to a data library like TanStack Query or a framework's server-side fetching rather than raw effects.
answerGeneralTr: Bir function component'te veri çekme bir useEffect'e aittir; tipik olarak boş bir dependency dizisiyle, böylece mount'tan sonra bir kez çalışır — eski componentDidMount'un karşılığı. Sonucu state'e koyarsın ve cleanup'ı (request'i iptal etmeyi) effect'in return'ünde ele alırsın, böylece hızlı bir unmount gitmiş bir component üzerinde state ayarlamaz. Pratikte çoğu uygulama bunu ham effect'ler yerine TanStack Query gibi bir veri kütüphanesine ya da bir framework'ün server-side fetching'ine devreder.
